title: The LLM stopped calling. The tool never did.
summary: Model-call limits can stop an agent loop, but they do not stop generated code or a tool process that loops forever inside a sandbox.
symptoms: The orchestration layer shows one tool call in-flight for minutes while the LLM call count stays below its configured limit.
The sandbox consumes CPU or memory continuously, but no new model or tool invocation is recorded.
The user cancels the task, yet the child process continues running until the worker or container is killed.
failure_boundary: The dangerous boundary is the hand-off from the agent runtime to executable code. Before the call, the orchestrator owns termination. After the call starts, a model-step limit is irrelevant unless a separate sandbox supervisor can independently stop the process.
why: Teams often protect the outer loop with max model calls, max agent steps, token budgets or API-level limits. Those controls help when the model repeatedly invokes tools. They do not help when a single invocation starts code containing an infinite loop, deadlock, blocking network call, runaway recursion, child-process storm or unbounded output. From the orchestrator's point of view there may be only one perfectly valid tool call that never returns.
example: A code-execution tool receives generated Python that retries an empty work queue with `while True`. The agent made only one tool call, so its 20-call budget never moves. The sandbox process keeps one CPU core busy for an hour. A model-side stop condition cannot see or terminate the loop because execution has already crossed into a different process boundary.
fooled: Relying on a maximum number of LLM calls or agent steps as the primary loop control.
Assuming an HTTP 4xx/5xx limit from the model gateway protects code that is already running.
Sending a cancellation flag to the model while leaving the sandbox process tree alive.
Using a cooperative timeout inside generated code as the only termination mechanism.
prevent: Run generated or untrusted code in a separate process/container, never in the agent worker process.
Enforce an external wall-clock TTL per tool invocation and an overall task deadline.
Apply CPU-time, memory, PID/thread, file-descriptor, disk, output-byte and network-request limits at the sandbox boundary.
Prefer narrow deterministic tools over arbitrary code execution when the task does not require a general sandbox.
Pass cancellation/deadline context to well-behaved tools, but treat it as an optimization rather than the hard safety boundary.
detect: Track wall-clock duration and CPU seconds for every in-flight tool invocation.
Require heartbeat or progress events for long-running tools and alert on progress silence.
Watch sandbox RSS, process count, output growth and child-process tree—not only LLM request count.
Record the code/tool hash so repeated hangs from the same artifact can be quarantined.
recover: On deadline: send graceful termination, wait a short bounded grace period, then kill the entire process group/container.
Destroy the sandbox after a hard timeout rather than returning it to the pool in an unknown state.
Mark the workflow as TOOL_TIMEOUT or TOOL_KILLED instead of pretending the tool returned a normal error.
Before retrying a timed-out write-capable tool, reconcile whether an external side effect happened.
Cap retries and escalate or quarantine repeated executions of the same failing code.
test: A tight `while True` CPU loop.
Infinite recursion or uncontrolled memory growth.
A sleeping or blocked network call that never returns.
Unbounded stdout/log generation.
A child-process storm.
A tool that commits an external side effect and then hangs before returning.
watch: timeouts retried after possible side effects
invariant: Every tool invocation has an owner outside the tool that can terminate its full process tree within a bounded time.
closing: An agent-step limit controls the agent. A sandbox deadline controls the code. Production systems need both.

title: One inference region failed. Traffic kept going there.
summary: A multi-region model deployment is not resilient if the router keeps sending requests to an unhealthy endpoint.
symptoms: Only a portion of model requests return 5xx or timeout errors.
Healthy regions still have capacity, but user failures continue.
Removing one endpoint from routing immediately improves success rate.
failure_boundary: The model may be healthy in five regions and broken in one; the failure becomes product-wide only when routing cannot distinguish those states quickly enough.
why: Static round-robin pools spread traffic, but they also spread regional failures. Model gateways need active health, failure-rate windows and enough spare capacity to eject a bad region without overloading the survivors.
example: An AI service uses six inference regions. One region starts returning 503s after a provider-side routing change. Five regions remain healthy, yet one-sixth of traffic continues failing because the endpoint stays in the pool until someone changes configuration manually.
fooled: Calling a deployment 'multi-region' without testing regional evacuation.
Using DNS reachability as the only health signal.
Immediately returning a recovered region to full traffic.
Running every healthy region near capacity, leaving no room for failover.
prevent: Route through a model gateway with per-region health state and endpoint ejection.
Reserve failover headroom instead of operating every region at saturation.
Use region-specific circuit breakers and bounded retry policies.
Keep provider and deployment configuration versioned and centrally observable.
detect: Break down success rate, 5xx, latency and throttling by region/deployment.
Run synthetic inference probes independent of user traffic.
Compare router decisions with endpoint health and capacity.
recover: Eject the unhealthy region automatically after a bounded failure threshold.
Shift traffic only to regions with confirmed capacity.
Reintroduce the region gradually with canary traffic after recovery.
test: Force one region to return 503 while production-like traffic is flowing.
Simulate one slow region rather than a clean outage.
Recover the region and verify controlled re-entry rather than an immediate traffic flood.
invariant: Loss of one inference region must not become loss of the AI product when healthy capacity still exists.
closing: Redundancy is inventory. Resilience is the ability to stop sending work to the broken copy.

title: The model existed in config. The provider said 404.
summary: Your control plane can say a deployment is active after the provider has removed, renamed or retired the actual serving resource.
symptoms: Agents repeatedly request a model deployment that no longer exists.
Database or configuration records still show the model as enabled.
The failure persists across application restarts because the wrong state is durable.
failure_boundary: Two control planes disagree: your catalog says 'available' while the provider's serving plane says 'not found'. The application cannot repair that contradiction with retries.
why: Model catalogs are often copied into databases, feature flags and agent configuration. Provider-side changes happen independently. Without reconciliation, stale control-plane state can outlive the deployment it references.
example: A team removes an old dedicated model deployment during a migration, but several agents still reference its deployment key in durable configuration. Every request gets a deterministic 404. Retries increase load but cannot recreate a resource that no longer exists.
fooled: Retrying a deterministic 'deployment not found' error.
Validating model configuration only when an agent is created.
Treating database state as the source of truth for provider inventory.
Deleting an old deployment before proving zero active references.
prevent: Maintain a reconciler between internal model catalog state and provider inventory.
Block deletion/retirement while active references remain.
Validate deployment existence during release and agent activation.
Use staged deprecation: announce, migrate, drain, verify, then remove.
detect: Alert on deterministic model-not-found errors separately from transient failures.
Continuously compare configured deployment IDs with provider inventory.
Track active agents by deployment/version before migration.
recover: Stop retrying the missing deployment.
Route to a pre-validated compatible deployment when policy allows.
Repair the control-plane reference and verify all consumers converge.
test: Remove a test deployment while references still exist and verify the reconciler catches it.
Rename/version a deployment and confirm pre-release validation blocks stale references.
Exercise rollback to the previous valid deployment mapping.
invariant: Every enabled model reference must resolve to a serving deployment that the runtime can actually call.
closing: A model name in a database is not a serving model. Reconcile control-plane truth with provider truth.

title: The primary model hit capacity. The workflow had nowhere to go.
summary: Token, concurrency or quota pressure becomes a business outage when no degraded mode or validated fallback path exists.
symptoms: Error rate rises sharply only during traffic spikes.
Requests exceed model concurrency, token or throughput limits.
Work falls back to manual handling because every overload request fails outright.
failure_boundary: Capacity failure is expected behavior from a bounded provider. The architectural failure is having only one admissible execution path when that bound is reached.
why: Inference capacity is not infinitely elastic. Dedicated capacity, shared quotas and model-specific limits can all saturate. Blind retries make pressure worse. Fallback must be designed before the incident—and validated because another model may behave differently.
example: An AI processing service normally uses a preferred high-capability model. A morning spike exceeds its concurrency allowance. With no admission control or compatible fallback, every excess request fails and a backlog forms faster than humans can absorb it.
fooled: Treating overload as a transient error and immediately retrying.
Assuming a smaller model is automatically behaviorally compatible.
Failing open into an unlimited queue with no age or capacity policy.
Testing fallback only for response syntax, not task correctness.
prevent: Use admission control and explicit per-model concurrency/token budgets.
Pre-register fallback models and validate them on workflow-specific evals.
Define degraded modes: lower-cost model, reduced context, read-only mode, queued execution or human path.
Keep queue size/age bounded and expose backpressure upstream.
detect: Track quota utilization, concurrency, token throughput, throttling and queue age.
Distinguish provider overload from application bugs.
Measure quality and tool-choice drift when fallback activates.
recover: Shed or defer low-priority work before critical work.
Route eligible tasks to validated fallback capacity.
Drain backlog at a controlled rate after capacity returns.
test: Artificially lower primary-model capacity and verify automatic degradation.
Run the same golden workflow suite on every fallback model.
Test recovery while a backlog already exists.
invariant: A bounded model tier must produce a bounded, intentional degraded mode—not an uncontrolled outage.
closing: Fallback is not a model name in config. It is a tested alternate operating mode.

title: The next message landed on another worker—and the conversation disappeared.
summary: Session affinity can hide state design problems until traffic crosses workers, zones or regions.
symptoms: Follow-up questions are treated as new conversations.
The issue appears intermittently or only after scaling/failover.
A single-node environment works perfectly while multi-node production loses context.
failure_boundary: If conversation correctness depends on process-local memory, any routing change becomes a semantic failure.
why: Sticky sessions can keep requests on one worker, but they are not durable state. Workers restart, regions fail and autoscaling moves traffic. Sequence numbers, conversation state and control flags need a shared source of truth if the workflow requires continuity.
example: A user asks a follow-up question. The load balancer sends it to a different data centre whose worker has no in-memory history for that conversation. The model receives a valid request—but without the prior turns needed to interpret it.
fooled: Using stickiness as the only persistence mechanism.
Assuming conversation ID alone means the state exists everywhere.
Failing to version or sequence messages.
Testing only on one replica.
prevent: Persist canonical conversation/workflow state outside the worker.
Use session affinity only as a latency optimization.
Carry a stable conversation ID plus monotonic sequence/version.
Make state reconstruction deterministic across workers and regions.
detect: Log routing target, conversation version and state source for every turn.
Alert on sequence gaps, missing context and unexpected new-session creation.
Compare same-session requests across replicas.
recover: Reload the latest durable state on a routing miss.
Reject or reconcile stale/out-of-order updates rather than silently overwriting newer state.
Rebuild transient caches from durable history.
test: Force every consecutive turn onto a different worker.
Restart the worker between two turns.
Replay out-of-order and duplicate messages.
Fail over between regions mid-conversation.
invariant: Any healthy worker that receives a valid conversation ID can reconstruct the state required to continue correctly.
closing: Stickiness can improve locality. It should never be the thing preserving memory.

title: Security rotated the credential. The running agent kept the old one.
summary: Credential rotation improves security, but long-lived workers fail if identity is loaded once and treated as permanent.
symptoms: A previously healthy tool suddenly returns authentication failures after a planned rotation.
Restarting or reloading the worker fixes the issue.
Only long-running agents fail while newly started workers succeed.
failure_boundary: The external identity changed while the agent process stayed alive. A secret file update is not enough if the running process never refreshes what it already loaded.
why: Agents can live much longer than ordinary request handlers. They may cache passwords, tokens or secret-derived clients for hours. Rotation creates two versions of reality: the secret manager has the new credential while the process still holds the old one.
example: An overnight data agent authenticates successfully at startup. A scheduled credential rotation happens two hours later. New processes use the updated credential, but the long-running worker keeps reusing the stale client and every API call begins failing.
fooled: Assuming updating a secret store automatically updates process memory.
Treating all 401/403 responses as permanent authorization denial.
Embedding credentials in static configuration.
Restarting the whole platform as the normal rotation strategy.
prevent: Prefer short-lived credentials or workload identity where possible.
Read secrets through a version-aware provider instead of static config.
Refresh before expiry and on classified authentication failure.
Design client/session recreation without restarting the whole workflow.
detect: Expose credential version/lease age without logging the secret.
Correlate auth failures with rotation events.
Alert when running workers hold a superseded credential version.
recover: Invalidate the stale client and fetch the latest credential.
Retry only after identity refresh and within a bounded policy.
Checkpoint long-running work so auth recovery does not restart the job from zero.
test: Rotate credentials while a long-running task is active.
Revoke the old credential immediately and verify refresh.
Simulate secret-manager unavailability during rotation.
invariant: A running agent must be able to survive authorized identity rotation without manual restart or use of stale authority.
closing: Secret rotation is not complete when the vault changes. It is complete when every live consumer converges.

title: Two valid triggers started processing the same work.
summary: A webhook and a poller can both be correct individually and still create duplicate or conflicting execution paths together.
symptoms: Users receive duplicate actions or replies.
One consumer makes work disappear before the intended consumer sees it.
Disabling either trigger makes the problem vanish.
failure_boundary: The failure is ownership. Two independently valid consumers both believe they are responsible for the same external event.
why: Teams often add a faster event path without fully retiring the old scheduled path. If both consume the same mailbox, queue, record or status transition, timing decides which workflow wins. Idempotency helps, but the architecture still needs an explicit owner.
example: A scheduled poller is designed to process unread requests every few minutes. Later, a real-time webhook is enabled for the same source. The webhook responds first and changes the source state; when the poller runs, the item no longer matches its query—or both paths perform separate side effects.
fooled: Assuming two consumers are safe because both are individually idempotent.
Using source state such as 'unread' as the only ownership mechanism.
Renewing obsolete subscriptions automatically.
Failing to record which trigger claimed an event.
prevent: Choose one authoritative ingestion path per event class, or explicitly coordinate multiple paths.
Assign a stable event ID and durable deduplication record.
Use leases/fencing or an inbox table when only one consumer may own work.
Make trigger lifecycle visible and auditable.
detect: Trace event ID across every trigger and consumer.
Alert on multiple claims for the same event.
Inventory active webhooks, pollers and schedules continuously.
recover: Disable the unintended path and stop automatic renewal.
Reconcile external side effects before replaying missed events.
Backfill from the source of truth with dedupe enabled.
test: Fire webhook and poller simultaneously for the same event.
Delay one consumer so ordering reverses.
Restart a consumer after claim but before completion.
invariant: For every external event, the system can identify the single execution owner—or prove that multiple consumers are safe.
closing: Two correct pipelines can make one incorrect system when ownership is implicit.

title: One RAG feature flag turned a query into thousands of clauses.
summary: Hybrid retrieval and query expansion can exceed engine limits even when the user's question is small.
symptoms: Search fails with a maximum-clause or query-complexity error.
The failure appears only for certain filters, expansions or feature flags.
Removing one retrieval mode immediately restores service.
failure_boundary: The user query is small, but the generated search plan is not. Complexity is created between orchestration and the search engine.
why: Hybrid retrieval may combine rewritten queries, metadata filters, synonym expansion, lexical clauses, vector searches and tenant restrictions. Each layer can multiply the final query. Search engines have hard limits, so query shape must be treated as a budgeted resource.
example: A retrieval feature enables multiple rewrites and expands metadata conditions for a large entitlement set. The final search request contains several thousand Boolean clauses and the engine rejects it before retrieval begins.
fooled: Looking only at user-query length.
Increasing engine limits instead of bounding query construction.
Enabling hybrid retrieval globally without slice testing.
Logging the original question but not the final generated search plan.
prevent: Define a query-complexity budget before sending work to the search engine.
Cap rewrites, filter expansions, synonyms and Boolean clause count.
Use set-based/lookup filters where supported instead of giant OR lists.
Provide a simpler retrieval fallback when the planned query exceeds budget.
detect: Log clause count, rewrite count, filter cardinality and final serialized query size.
Slice failures by retrieval mode, tenant and feature flag.
Alert before hard engine limits are reached.
recover: Retry with a bounded fallback query, not the identical oversized request.
Disable the offending expansion path through a safe feature switch.
Preserve the failed query plan for debugging and regression tests.
test: Large entitlement/filter sets.
Worst-case synonym and rewrite expansion.
Hybrid search with maximum metadata cardinality.
Fallback behavior when the query budget is exceeded.
invariant: No generated retrieval plan reaches the search engine without passing a bounded complexity check.
closing: RAG can fail before retrieval. Measure the query you actually send, not only the question the user typed.

title: The model was fast. A downstream dependency made the AI look slow.
summary: Database locks, bad query plans and other dependencies can dominate end-to-end latency while model telemetry stays healthy.
symptoms: Model latency remains normal while total request latency climbs.
Multiple AI features slow down at the same time.
Killing a blocking database session or changing a query plan restores performance immediately.
failure_boundary: Users experience one AI request, but the critical path crosses model, retrieval, databases, tools and network dependencies. The slowest layer owns the experience.
why: AI observability is often model-centric. That makes it easy to over-investigate tokens, context and provider latency while a conventional dependency is holding locks or running a pathological plan.
example: An agent service reads prompt/configuration metadata before every model call. A blocking database session holds a hot table lock. The LLM responds quickly once invoked, but most requests spend their time waiting before inference even starts.
fooled: Using model latency as a proxy for user latency.
Looking at service averages instead of critical-path spans.
Restarting AI workers when the bottleneck is shared infrastructure.
Ignoring database plan changes because the application code did not change.
prevent: Instrument end-to-end traces with separate spans for model, retrieval, DB, tools and queue wait.
Set dependency-specific timeouts and bulkheads.
Use appropriate indexes and query-plan controls for critical metadata paths.
Keep expensive administrative/reporting work away from latency-sensitive paths.
detect: Monitor lock waits, connection-pool saturation, query-plan changes and DB time inside AI traces.
Compare model-service time with total user latency.
Alert on dependency contribution, not only total latency.
recover: Remove the blocking workload or force a known-good query plan where appropriate.
Degrade non-critical reads if safe.
Drain queued work gradually after the dependency recovers.
test: Inject DB latency and lock contention.
Change a query plan in staging and compare critical-path traces.
Exhaust the connection pool while inference remains healthy.
invariant: Every user-visible AI latency regression can be decomposed into owned time across the full critical path.
closing: An AI system is still a distributed system. Sometimes the least glamorous dependency is the one users are waiting on.

title: The safety check failed because one of its own dependencies was down.
summary: A guardrail is part of the production dependency graph; its outage policy must be explicit before the dependency fails.
symptoms: Agent requests fail because the policy/guardrail service cannot reach an upstream dependency.
Teams debate during the incident whether to bypass the safety layer.
Low-risk and high-risk actions are blocked identically.
failure_boundary: When the safety decision is unavailable, the runtime still has to choose: fail closed, fail open, or enter a limited degraded mode. That choice is security policy—not an exception handler.
why: Guardrails may rely on identity, policy stores, classification services or third-party APIs. If the entire system assumes those dependencies are always available, an upstream outage can either stop the product or tempt operators to bypass controls under pressure.
example: A policy check depends on an external identity/data service. That service has a regional outage. Read-only summarization and high-impact write actions now both receive the same 'guardrail unavailable' error even though their risk is very different.
fooled: Treating guardrails as stateless prompt text instead of a service dependency.
Using one global fail-open/fail-closed decision for every action class.
Allowing emergency bypasses that are not scoped, logged and time-bounded.
Testing malicious prompts but never testing guardrail infrastructure failure.
prevent: Define availability policy by action risk: read, propose, reversible write, irreversible write.
Keep high-impact authorization enforcement in the runtime even when auxiliary classifiers are unavailable.
Cache only policies that are safe to use with explicit version/expiry semantics.
Reduce correlated dependencies between the agent and the service that authorizes it.
detect: Separate 'request denied' from 'policy decision unavailable'.
Trace which upstream dependency prevented the guardrail decision.
Alert on bypass/degraded-mode activation.
recover: Enter a pre-defined degraded mode rather than improvising during the outage.
Keep risky writes blocked unless an alternate authoritative control exists.
Revalidate deferred actions after policy service recovery.
test: Take the guardrail dependency offline during read-only tasks.
Repeat for reversible and irreversible actions.
Expire cached policy while the dependency is unavailable.
Verify emergency override scope, audit and automatic expiry.
invariant: Loss of a safety dependency must never silently grant more authority than the healthy system would allow.
closing: The guardrail has a failure mode too. Design that mode before someone asks to bypass it at 2 a.m.

title: The upgrade was 'compatible'—until the agent actually ran.
summary: Platform, security or library changes can preserve an API shape while breaking runtime behavior that an agent workflow depends on.
symptoms: A previously working tool fails only after a platform/security/dependency rollout.
The schema still validates, but loading or executing the capability fails.
Only a subset of hosts/pods fail because their runtime state differs.
failure_boundary: Static compatibility answers whether interfaces still look acceptable. Agent behavioral compatibility asks whether the complete workflow still executes correctly under the new runtime.
why: Agent systems sit on dynamic layers: Python packages, JVM class loading, sandbox policies, tool allowlists, MCP/tool schemas and provider behavior. A change can be 'valid' locally yet alter imports, serialization, permissions or execution semantics in production.
example: A security update narrows the set of allowed function types. Existing agent configuration still parses successfully, but one tool type is no longer executable. In another case, only hosts that received a runtime package patch fail during spreadsheet processing.
fooled: Equating schema compatibility with workflow compatibility.
Rolling infrastructure or dependency changes everywhere at once.
Testing tool registration without executing representative workflows.
Ignoring host-level drift because the application version is identical.
prevent: Pin and version runtime dependencies, sandbox policy and tool contracts alongside agent code.
Maintain a compatibility manifest for model/tool/runtime versions.
Run state-verified workflow regressions before platform changes.
Use canary hosts/pods and staged rollout with fast rollback.
detect: Compare failures by host, runtime version, policy version and dependency fingerprint.
Run synthetic tool executions, not only health endpoints.
Alert on deserialization/import/class-loading/policy-denial regressions after changes.
recover: Rollback the runtime/policy change or migrate the affected tool to a supported contract.
Restart/recreate only the contaminated runtime when state can be safely reconstructed.
Capture the failing workflow as a permanent regression case.
test: Upgrade one dependency while keeping agent code unchanged.
Change sandbox/tool allowlists.
Run the same workflow across old/new hosts and compare final state.
Verify that rollback restores behavior, not just process health.
invariant: A release is compatible only when previously supported agent workflows still reach the expected externally verified state.
closing: Software compatibility is necessary. For agents, behavioral compatibility is the production guarantee that matters.
